questions.question: In letter-shift coding, if CAT is coded as DBU, what rule is being applied?
options: Each letter is shifted forward by 1 position
Each letter is replaced by its mirror letter
Each letter is replaced by a number
questions.rationale: C->D, A->B, T->U — each letter moves forward exactly one position in the alphabet, a uniform +1 shift.

questions.question: What happens when a letter-shift rule pushes a letter past Z (e.g., Y + 3)?
options: It wraps around to the start of the alphabet (A, B, C...)
It becomes a number instead of a letter
The question has no valid answer
questions.rationale: The alphabet is treated as a loop of 26 letters, so shifting past Z wraps around back to A, then B, and so on.

questions.question: In substitution/mirror coding where A<->Z, B<->Y, C<->X and so on, what is true about each mapped pair's positions?
questions.rationale: Mirror coding reflects each letter's position around the alphabet's center, so a letter at position p maps to position 27-p, meaning every mapped pair sums to 27.

questions.question: Why is it important to verify a coding rule against every letter of the given example, not just the first one or two?
options: It isn't important — the first letter is always enough
Some questions apply a non-uniform rule, or an exception on one letter, that only shows up later in the word
Longer words always use number coding instead
It only matters for reverse coding
questions.rationale: Some coding questions mix a shift with an exception on a specific letter (often the last or a repeated one) — checking only the first letters can lead to applying the wrong rule to the new word.

questions.question: Using the rule 'position + 2, written as a digit', how would the letter C (position 3) be coded?
questions.rationale: C is at position 3; adding 2 gives 5, so C is coded as 5 under this rule.

questions.question: What is FLOWER coded as under simple reverse (mirror-of-order) coding, with no letter shift?
questions.rationale: Reverse coding simply reads the word's letters backward: F-L-O-W-E-R reversed is R-E-W-O-L-F, i.e., REWOLF.

questions.question: In matrix/coordinate-based coding, a letter's code is typically written as what?
questions.rationale: Matrix-style coding places letters in a grid and codes each one using its row-and-column coordinates within that grid.

questions.question: If DELHI is coded as EFMIJ (each letter shifted +1), how is MUMBAI coded under the same rule?
questions.rationale: Shifting each letter of MUMBAI forward by 1: M->N, U->V, M->N, B->C, A->B, I->J, giving NVNCBJ.

questions.question: What is one of the most common mistakes in letter-shift coding problems?
options: Forgetting alphabet wrap-around (e.g., that Z + 1 = A)
Checking the rule against every letter
Writing out the alphabet with positions
questions.rationale: Forgetting that the alphabet wraps around at Z (back to A) is one of the most common sources of error in letter-shift coding.

questions.question: What is generally the fastest way to identify which coding type a question uses?
options: Guess based on how the word looks
Compare the output letters/numbers systematically against the input, starting with the simplest rule types (shift, mirror) before more complex ones
Only look at the first letter
questions.rationale: Systematically comparing input and output, starting with simple checks (shift, mirror) before considering more complex rule types, is the most reliable way to quickly identify the coding pattern.
